prompt: Why is the shared repository created with git init --bare?
hint: Nobody edits files in it.

choices.text: It has no working tree
choices.why: Right. Everybody works in their own copy, so it only holds what is inside .git.

choices.text: Bare repositories are faster to clone
choices.why: Speed is not the reason. There is simply no folder of files to keep in step.

choices.text: It stops anybody pushing to it
choices.why: Everybody pushes to it; that is its job.

choices.text: It hides the history from the team
choices.why: It holds the whole history, like every copy.

prompt: What is special about the name origin?
hint: Could a team call it something else?

choices.text: It is the only name Git accepts for a remote
choices.why: Any name works; git remote add takes whatever you give it.

choices.text: Nothing; it is a convention
choices.why: Right. It is the name clone gives, and everybody keeps it.

choices.text: It marks the repository that owns the history
choices.why: No copy owns the history; every copy is complete.

choices.text: It makes pushes go to GitHub
choices.why: The address decides where pushes go; the name is a label.

prompt: What did -u add to git push -u origin main?
hint: Read the last line of the output.

choices.text: It made the push faster
choices.why: -u changes nothing about the transfer.

choices.text: It sent every branch, not only main
choices.why: It sent main. -u is about what happens next time.

choices.text: It forced the push through
choices.why: Forcing is --force, and nothing needed forcing here.

choices.text: main now tracks origin/main
choices.why: Right. So a plain push or pull needs no names. It is needed once per new branch.

prompt: What did git clone ~/remotes/site.git give Bruno? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of these belongs to his settings, which a clone does not copy.

choices.text: Every commit of the repository
choices.why: Yes. A clone is a complete copy.

choices.text: A remote called origin pointing at the shared copy
choices.why: Yes. That is where the name comes from.

choices.text: Ana's name as the author of his commits
choices.why: Authorship comes from settings, and he set his own in the clone.

choices.text: A working tree with main checked out
choices.why: Yes. Unlike the bare copy, his has files to edit.

prompt: Bruno pushed a commit. Ana's git status still says "Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'". Why?
hint: What is status comparing with?

choices.text: Bruno's push failed
choices.why: It succeeded: main moved on origin.

choices.text: Her record of origin is out of date
choices.why: Right. Git never contacts origin unless a command does.

choices.text: Status only looks at files, not commits
choices.why: It compares branches too; the second line is exactly that comparison.

choices.text: Ana's copy updates itself every few minutes
choices.why: If it did, it would have seen the push. Nothing happens on its own.

prompt: What does git fetch change in Ana's repository?
hint: Her own main did not move.

choices.text: Brings commits, moves origin/main
choices.why: Right. Her branch and her files are untouched.

choices.text: It moves main to match origin
choices.why: That is the second half of pull, not fetch.

choices.text: It sends her commits to origin
choices.why: That is push. Fetch only brings things in.

choices.text: It rewrites her files to origin's version
choices.why: No file changes on a fetch.

prompt: git pull is git ___ followed by bringing origin/main into main.
hint: The safe half.

prompt: Match each command to what it does.
hint: Only one of them sends anything.

pairs.right: Brings commits in and moves origin/main only
Brings commits in and joins them to your branch
Sends your commits and moves the remote's branch

right_distractors: Checks origin in the background for new work

prompt: Ana's push was rejected with (fetch first). What does origin have that she does not?
hint: Somebody pushed before her.

choices.text: A commit of Bruno's she lacks
choices.why: Right. Moving main to her commit would drop his.

choices.text: A newer version of Git than hers
choices.why: Versions have nothing to do with it; the branch has moved.

choices.text: A lock that another person placed on main
choices.why: There is no lock. There is a commit she has not got.

choices.text: A tag with her name on it
choices.why: No tag is involved in this refusal.

prompt: Why does a push only ever move a branch forward?
hint: What would a backward move lose?

choices.text: Anywhere else would drop commits
choices.why: Right. Forward means every commit that was there is still in the history.

choices.text: Because remotes store only the newest commit
choices.why: A remote holds the whole history like any copy.

choices.text: Because Git cannot compare two histories
choices.why: It compares them to decide whether the move is forward.

choices.text: Because tags would stop pointing at their commits
choices.why: Tags point at commits, not at branches; they would not move.

prompt: After the rejection, git pull fetched and then stopped with fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches. Why?
hint: There are two ways to join, from lesson 6.

choices.text: The fetch failed
choices.why: It worked: Bruno's commit arrived before the question.

choices.text: It won't choose merge or rebase
choices.why: Right. Both sides have new commits, and there are two ways to join them. It refuses until it is told, by an option or a setting.

choices.text: Pull only works on a clean working tree
choices.why: Her working tree was clean. The issue is the diverged history.

choices.text: She must be the one who pushed last
choices.why: No such rule exists.

prompt: Match each option of git pull to how it joins diverged branches.
hint: One refuses to join at all.

pairs.right: Replays your unpushed commits on top of origin/main
Merges origin/main in with a merge commit
Accepts only a fast-forward and refuses otherwise

prompt: Why does git pull --rebase not break lesson 6's rule about rebasing shared commits?
hint: Which commits get replayed?

choices.text: It only rewrites your commits that nobody has yet
choices.why: Right. Bruno's commit is left exactly as it was.

choices.text: It asks the remote for permission first
choices.why: No permission is involved; it is about which commits move.

choices.text: It rebases origin/main onto your branch instead
choices.why: The other way round, and that would rewrite shared commits.

choices.text: Pull always merges underneath
choices.why: --rebase really rebases. The safety is in what it rebases.

prompt: A colleague's advice for a rejected push is git push --force. What would that do on a shared branch?
hint: The rejection existed to prevent something.

choices.text: Merge the two histories on the server
choices.why: Force merges nothing. It replaces.

choices.text: Drop Bruno's commit from main
choices.why: Right. It moves the branch to her commit. Exactly what the rejection was protecting against.

choices.text: Push only the commits that do not conflict
choices.why: Force sends her branch as it is, whatever it drops.

choices.text: Nothing, since servers ignore --force
choices.why: It works, which is the danger. Some hosts can forbid it on a branch.

prompt: What is the difference between a tag and a branch?
hint: One of them moves with each commit.

choices.text: A tag is a name that never moves
choices.why: Right. It marks one commit for good.

choices.text: A tag holds a copy of the files
choices.why: It names a commit; the commit's tree holds the files.

choices.text: A tag can only be made on main
choices.why: Any commit can be tagged.

choices.text: A tag is local and cannot be shared
choices.why: It can: git push origin v1.0 did.

prompt: Ana runs git tag -a v1.0 and then git push. Is v1.0 on origin?
hint: What does a plain push send?

choices.text: Yes, tags always travel with commits
choices.why: A plain push sends branches only.

choices.text: Yes, if it was annotated
choices.why: Annotated or not, it needs its own push.

choices.text: No; tags are pushed on their own
choices.why: Right. git push origin v1.0 sends it, or --tags sends them all.

choices.text: No, tags can never be pushed
choices.why: They can, separately.

prompt: A release fixes a wrong price and changes nothing else. The last release was v1.4.2. Following semantic versioning, what is the new tag?
hint: A fix moves the last number.

choices.why: The first number is for changes that break something that worked.
The middle number is for something new. This is a fix.
Right. major.minor.patch, and a fix is a patch.

choices.text: v1.4.2, moved to the new commit
choices.why: Moving a published tag gives one version to two commits.

prompt: To delete the branch autumn-menu from the shared copy: git push origin ___ autumn-menu
hint: The option says what to do to it.

prompt: Ana's morning with a shared repository. Put it in order.
hint: Other people's work first, your own last.
items: git pull, to start from what the others did
Edit and commit her own change
git pull --rebase, in case somebody pushed meanwhile
trap: Pushing before pulling again is how a push gets rejected.

prompt: Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of them imagine Git doing things on its own.

choices.text: origin/main moves only when you talk to origin
choices.why: Yes: on fetch, pull and push.

choices.text: Git checks origin for new commits in the background
choices.why: It never does. Until you fetch, it does not know.

choices.text: A rejected push leaves the remote exactly as it was
choices.why: Yes. Nothing is half-sent.

choices.text: A remote can be a folder on the same machine
choices.why: Yes. Only the address differs from a URL.

choices.text: Pushing a branch also pushes its tags
choices.why: Tags are pushed separately.
